correctness.rationale: Orthogonal projection restricts support functions. The planar support-area formula gives derivative equal to the great-circle integral. The three-dimensional surface-area density is det(nabla^2 h+hI); linearizing at the unit sphere gives Delta f+2f, whose Laplacian term integrates to zero. The resulting equatorial Funk transform on S^3 has harmonic multiplier 4*pi*C_l^1(0)/C_l^1(1), and C_l^1(0)=sin((l+1)pi/2), so its kernel is exactly the odd functions. Odd functions integrate to zero on every great circle, proving the implication. The packaged checker replays all nontrivial algebraic identities.

originality.rationale: Problem 4 in the 2009 Banach Center Open Problem Session explicitly identifies the noninjective Grassmann Radon map as the obstacle and asks whether projection-area functions avoid its kernel. Goodey's 2009 survey develops the relevant projection-function and harmonic framework without stating the tangent-range result. Goodey's materially inspected 1998 full text proves global Radon uniqueness for centrally symmetric bodies and polytopes but does not state or imply the differential implication for arbitrary asymmetric perturbations. Targeted statement and alias searches found no covering theorem.
residual_risks: The harmonic ingredients are classical, so the tangent-range observation may exist implicitly or under different terminology in older geometric-tomography literature.
The theorem is first-order only and does not settle local nonlinear uniqueness.
No second-order kernel analysis is included.

value.rationale: The result addresses the exact obstruction singled out in a named open problem: although the ambient Grassmann Radon map has a kernel, that kernel contains no nonzero first-order projection-area data at the ball. This forces any smooth counterexample family through the ball to be genuinely nonlinear, beginning at second order or higher, and provides a concrete tangent-space target for local uniqueness or stability work.
